seo.title: AI Audio Research | Igor Szuniewicz
seo.description: Bachelor thesis: Can AI generate real-time sound effects for games?

header.title: Can AI generate game audio in real-time?
header.description: For my bachelor thesis I tried to answer one question: can AI generate sound effects fast enough for games? I built a Unity prototype that talks to AI models through a Python server. Short answer: not yet. But I found a workaround that actually works.

setup.title: What I tested and why
setup.intro: Every gunshot, footstep, and explosion in a game is a pre-recorded WAV file. Hundreds of them per project. AI could generate these on the fly, so every sound would be unique and adapted to the situation, no gigabytes of files shipping with the game. The catch: latency. If a sound arrives even 100ms late, players notice. That's the problem I set out to measure.
setup.approach: I built a prototype. Unity sends requests to a Python server, which calls an AI model and streams audio back. Tested three models: ElevenLabs (cloud API, best quality, latency all over the place), MMAudio (video-to-audio model I hacked to work for games, runs locally), and AudioGen (Meta's text-to-audio, most consistent but still too slow).

results.title: Measured Latency
results.subtitle: Generation times for each model vs. what games actually need. Log scale because the gaps are enormous.

tooltip.elevenlabs: Cloud API. Best quality, but latency jumps wildly: 1s to 12s on the same day.
tooltip.mmaudio: Video-to-audio model adapted for games. Runs locally, 2-5s per sound.
tooltip.audiogen: Meta's text-to-audio. Most consistent at ~3s, but that's still 3s too slow.
tooltip.cached: Pre-generated sounds served from memory. 21-55ms delivery.

elevenlabs.note: Cloud-based. Quality depends on server load that day.

mmaudio.note: Runs locally. Originally built for video soundtracks, not games.

audiogen.note: Most consistent of the three. Still 3 seconds too slow.

solution.title: Caching sounds ahead of time
solution.story: None of the models came close to real-time. The fastest was still over a second, roughly 60x too slow for a gunshot. I'd added a simple cache earlier just to avoid regenerating the same sound twice. Then I looked at the delivery times in the logs. 21-55ms. That's fast enough.
solution.insight: So I stopped trying to make AI faster and started thinking about when to generate instead. Load screens, quiet gameplay moments, menu screens. Cache the sounds. When the player pulls the trigger, serve from cache instantly and queue a replacement in the background.

loading.label: Loading screen
loading.description: AI generates sounds in the background while the player waits

cache.label: Cache ready
cache.description: 10 shots, 5 explosions, 8 footsteps, all sitting in memory

refill.label: Background refill
refill.description: System quietly generates replacements for next time

solution.usecases: Works best for predictable sounds: ambient audio, cutscene effects, weapons with limited fire rates. Falls apart for footsteps and other very frequent events where the cache empties faster than AI can refill it.

closing.conclusion: AI audio can't replace traditional sound design in games. Not yet. It's too slow for real-time. But cache sounds ahead of time and it can add variety and cut file sizes for the right use cases.
closing.reflection: The interesting part wasn't which model performed best. It was realizing that generation speed doesn't matter if you pick the right moment to generate. Even slow AI works when nobody's listening.

session2.title: Local AI Testing (Didn't Work)
session2.content: Tried running MusicGen and AudioLDM2 on student hardware. No GPU. 4 to 10 seconds per sound. Completely unusable for anything that needs quick feedback. Local-only generation is a dead end on this kind of hardware.

session4.title: Stress-Testing the Hybrid System
session4.content: Mixed procedural audio with cloud AI and hammered it: 100 simultaneous requests, all handled under 200ms. Hit 2253 generations per second at peak. The procedural path runs at 5ms, cloud path at 2-4 seconds. The hybrid approach holds up. It could ship.
